auditedPrs.notes: Squash commit 719aa88 on main. The PR cites no upstream Go, so it was read against its counterpart, the netstack link endpoint in wgengine/netstack, at the pinned commit e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55 (shallow fetch of that commit). The PR puts a 4096-packet, 4096*MTU-byte ring in front of both smoltcp netstacks, drops what does not fit, and leaves egress unbounded. Upstream does the opposite in both directions: no inbound queue, and a 512-slot blocking outbound queue. That gives two minor findings. They are the same two the earlier audit of this PR (#591) recorded; this pass re-derived them from the source and found nothing further. The bounding code itself is sound: every refusal path gives the byte budget back, and the new tests call the production pump_ingress and WakingPipe::ingress_bounded.

Squash commit 50611ab on main. It cites ipn/serve.go and ipn/ipnlocal/serve.go at e2ed432399c9b0fda7aa14e9eb27784d2d893c55, and was read against both, plus ipn/localapi/serve.go and client/local/serve.go for the wire form. Faithful: the five ServeConfig fields and their JSON tags, map-key ordering, HostPort.Port / net.SplitHostPort, expandProxyArg, parseRedirectWithCode, serveTypeFromPortHandler (HTTP tested before HTTPS, -1 as unknownServeType), and validateServeConfigUpdate with Go's message text and Go's test table (the two nil-config rows have no Rust form). Handler precedence follows tcpHandlerForServeTCP and serveWebHandler. The gaps are in two places. First, the lowering: the PR says anything served differently from Go is refused, but a Proxy at / and a Redirect are let through onto a runtime that does not serve them as Go does (three findings, one major). Second, the wire shape: Go's own form for 'no config' is null, which does not decode, and the encoding is not byte-for-byte for every string (two findings). The long list of shapes the PR refuses on purpose is filed once, as one minor finding, because Go serves all of them.

gate.detail: Scoped gate on main 3951752 with CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=4, RUST_TEST_THREADS=4 and TS_RS_EXPERIMENT set. Exit 0: cargo fmt --all -- --check on the pinned 1.95.0 toolchain; cargo run -p checks; cargo clippy --lib -D warnings and cargo clippy --bins --tests --benches --examples -D warnings -A missing_docs, both over the workspace minus ts_cli_util; cargo build --all-targets --all-features over the same scope. nextest over ts_control, ts_runtime, ts_netstack_smoltcp and the root crate exited 100: 1174 run, 1171 passed, 3 failed, 2 skipped. All three failures are socket tests this sandbox cannot run, and each failed on the network, not on an assertion about code: local_client_round_trips_through_the_localapi_server and localapi_server_authenticates_and_routes_over_real_socket ('Loopback(Os { code: 60, kind: TimedOut })'), and probe_stun_servers_once_sends_binding_request (no UDP: 'a STUN binding request must arrive at the v4 server: Elapsed'). The 2 skipped were filtered out because their loopback dial hangs here: serve_path_proxy_replays_consumed_head_to_backend and proxy_with_prefix_writes_prefix_before_bidi_copy. Every test #587 and #588 added passed. pass is true on that reading; it is not a claim that the three socket tests pass. Not run: the literal bin/check, which stops under set -e because --all-features does not compile ts_cli_util's tracy feature here and cargo deny refuses the banned aws-lc crates on any branch; and cargo doc, cargo deny, cargo machete and the doctests.

findings.title: A Proxy handler is lowered onto a raw byte splice, so client-sent Tailscale-User-* headers reach the backend and only the first request is routed
findings.detail: Upstream: serveWebHandler hands a Proxy handler to reverseProxy.ServeHTTP, an httputil.ReverseProxy that runs per request. Its Rewrite sets Out.Host to In.Host, calls addProxyForwardedHeaders (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-For) and addTailscaleIdentityHeaders. That last function first deletes any incoming Tailscale-User-Login, Tailscale-User-Name, Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic, Tailscale-Funnel-Request and Tailscale-Headers-Info ('Clear any incoming values squatting in the headers'), then sets them from WhoIs on the source address. addAppCapabilitiesHeader likewise deletes an incoming Tailscale-App-Capabilities. A backend dial failure is answered by the proxy with 502. Each request on a kept-alive connection goes through getServeHandler again. Merged: plan_http_handler (ts_control/src/serve/ipn.rs) lowers Proxy at mount / to ServeTarget::Proxy inside a Path mux, and proxy_backend_addr's comment says the backend is 'spliced verbatim the way Go's reverse proxy would forward it'. The runtime (serve_path and proxy_to_backend_with_prefix in ts_runtime/src/serve.rs) reads one request head, replays those bytes to the backend unchanged, then runs copy_bidirectional until the connection ends. So: (1) a tailnet peer can send its own Tailscale-User-Login or Tailscale-App-Capabilities header and the backend receives it as if the node had set it; Go guarantees a backend never sees a client-supplied value, and backends use these headers for identity. (2) No Tailscale-User-* or X-Forwarded-* header is ever added, so a backend that relies on them gets nothing. (3) After the first request, every later request on the same connection goes to that backend whatever its path, so with / as Proxy and /old as Redirect (the shape the PR's own test https_port_lowers_to_a_path_mux_with_its_hosts_cert builds) a second request for /old is proxied, not redirected. (4) A backend that cannot be dialed closes the connection with no response where Go answers 502. The PR refused Proxy with AcceptAppCaps for exactly this reason (the header is not produced) but let the plain Proxy through. By the PR's own rule ('refused, not approximated') a Proxy handler should be refused until the runtime parses and rewrites each request, or at least strips the Tailscale-* request headers.

findings.title: An HTTPS port answers any SNI name, where upstream refuses a handshake whose SNI has no Web entry
findings.detail: Upstream: getTLSServeCertForPort fails the handshake with 'no SNI ServerName' when the ClientHello has none, and with 'no webserver configured for name/port' unless webServerConfig finds a Web entry under the exact key net.JoinHostPort(hi.ServerName, port). getServeHandler then picks the handlers by r.TLS.ServerName again. serveTLSConfig is given serveTLSNextProtos(), so the port advertises ALPN h2 and http/1.1. Merged: plan_https picks the one Web entry whose key parses to the port (hp.port().ok() == Some(port)) and returns its host as cert_name. The acceptor built from it (tls_acceptor in ts_control/src/serve.rs) uses the SingleCert resolver, which returns that certificate for every ClientHello and never looks at the server name, and sets no ALPN protocols. So a client that sends no SNI, or a different name, completes the handshake and is routed to the handlers of the configured host, where Go ends the connection in the handshake. The PR refuses 'more than one SNI name per HTTPS port' because the runtime has one certificate per port, but the single-name case it lets through is not Go's either. Two smaller points on the same lookup: a Web key such as host:0443 is served here (the port is parsed) and never matches in Go (the key is compared as a string); and a client is never offered h2.

findings.title: A Redirect handler is let through, but the response is not what http.Redirect sends
findings.detail: Upstream: serveWebHandler calls http.Redirect(w, r, v, code) with the parsed target. http.Redirect makes a target with no scheme, no host and no leading slash absolute against the directory of the request path, cleans the path while keeping a trailing slash, hex-escapes non-ASCII bytes in Location, and for a GET writes a short text/html body with a link. The connection stays open for the next request. A CR or LF in the target is not refused; net/http writes it as a space. Merged: plan_http_handler lowers Redirect to ServeTarget::Redirect with the target copied as written, and serve_redirect (ts_runtime/src/serve.rs) writes 'Location: {to}' verbatim with Content-Length: 0 and Connection: close, then shuts the stream. So a target like 'new' or '/a/../b' or one with non-ASCII bytes yields a different Location header than Go's, a GET gets no body, the reason phrase for any status but 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 is the made-up 'Redirect', and the connection is closed after one response. serve_plan also refuses, as Invalid, two configs Go accepts and serves: a target containing CR or LF, and '301:' with nothing after the code. The PR refused Text because 'Go frames it as an HTTP response, the runtime writes bare bytes'; Redirect has the same kind of difference in a milder form and was not refused or listed.

findings.title: ServeState does not decode null, which is how upstream writes 'no serve config'
findings.detail: Upstream: a node with no serve config holds an invalid ServeConfigView. The LocalAPI GET handler serveServeConfig (ipn/localapi/serve.go) marshals that view, and ServeConfigView.MarshalJSON marshals the nil pointer, so the body is the four bytes null, not {}. The client decodes it into a *ipn.ServeConfig, which null leaves nil (getServeConfigFromJSON in client/local/serve.go). Clearing works the same way in reverse: Client.SetServeConfig(ctx, nil) posts null, and the handler decodes it into a fresh ipn.ServeConfig without error. The map values are pointers too (map[uint16]*TCPPortHandler, map[HostPort]*WebServerConfig, map[string]*HTTPHandler, the Services and Foreground maps), so Go decodes {"TCP":{"443":null}} to a nil entry, and GetWebHandler checks for sc.Web[hp] == nil. Merged: ServeState, TcpPortHandler, WebServerConfig, HttpHandler and ServiceConfig are plain derived structs. serde_json refuses null for a struct, so the document null fails to decode, and so does a null map value; only a null field is handled (the nullable helper). The test empty_object_decodes_to_the_empty_config_and_back says {} 'is what a fresh node's LocalAPI hands out', and the doc on Device::get_serve_config calls the never-set config 'Go's {}'. Both are wrong about upstream. The commit message's headline case was that Go's empty config did not decode; the form a Go node actually emits for it still does not. Also narrower than Go's decoder, the first admitted in the module doc and the second not: field names are matched case-sensitively where encoding/json matches them case-insensitively, and a repeated field name is an error where Go keeps the last.

findings.title: The encoding is not byte-for-byte Go's for every config, and the ETag check those bytes feed is not ported
findings.detail: Upstream: setServeConfigLocked takes an etag. When it is not empty it must equal generateServeConfigETag(prevConfig), the hex SHA-256 of json.Marshal of the stored config, or the call fails with ErrETagMismatch (HTTP 412 at the LocalAPI). The LocalAPI returns that value in the Etag header on GET, and the client sends it back as If-Match. json.Marshal escapes <, > and & (and U+2028, U+2029) inside strings as \u00XX, and writes a nil Handlers map as null because that field has no omitempty. Merged: the commit message and the test encodes_byte_for_byte_as_go_does state that ServeState 'encodes byte-for-byte as Go's json.Marshal does'. That holds for the fixture, but not in general: a Proxy or Redirect value with a query string ('https://host/?a=1&b=2') is written with a raw & where Go writes \u0026, and a Web entry decoded from {"Handlers":null} is written back as {"Handlers":{}}. The module doc of ts_control/src/serve/ipn.rs admits both and says ETag is not modelled because it is json:"-". The consequence is not stated there: a hash of this encoding is not Go's ETag for such a config, and Device::set_serve_config has no compare-and-swap at all, so two writers silently overwrite each other where Go returns ErrETagMismatch. The re-check added under the store lock only re-runs validate_serve_config_update; it does not detect that the stored config changed.

findings.title: set_serve_config refuses most of what an upstream ServeConfig can say
findings.detail: Upstream: setServeConfigLocked stores any config that passes validateServeConfigUpdate, and tcpHandlerForServeTCP, serveWebHandler and proxyHandlerForBackend then serve it: plain-HTTP ports; TCPForward with TerminateTLS, with ProxyProtocol, or to a unix: socket; Text; Path (files and directories); Redirect with ${HOST} and ${REQUEST_URI}; Proxy at any mount, with the mount prefix stripped; Proxy with AcceptAppCaps; Proxy to https://, https+insecure:// and unix: backends and to a backend URL with a path; several SNI names on one port; Services; Foreground; AllowFunnel. Upstream also stores, and answers at request time, configs this tree calls invalid: an HTTPS port with no Web entry (the handshake fails), a Web entry with no handlers (404), a handler with nothing set (500 'empty handler'), port 0, and a Web host outside the tailnet's names. Merged: ServeState::serve_plan returns Unsupported, Invalid or NotTailnetName for every one of these, and Device::set_serve_config maps each to BadRequest with the reason only in a warn log. What still runs is an HTTPS port with Proxy at / to a plain http:// host and literal Redirects, plus raw TCPForward to host:port. The refusals are deliberate, fail closed, and are listed in the commit message and the rustdoc, so this is recorded as one finding and not fourteen. It is a finding because the type now accepts and round-trips every upstream config while the node can run few of them, and a caller that gets BadRequest cannot tell which rule refused it without reading the log.

findings.title: Netstack ingress drops on a full ring, where upstream has no inbound queue and delivers synchronously
findings.detail: Upstream: netstack.go installs Impl.injectInbound as tstun's PostFilterPacketInboundFromWireGuard hook. For a packet the netstack should handle it calls linkEndpoint.gro, which ends in the dispatcher's DeliverNetworkPacket (linkEndpoint.injectInbound in link_endpoint.go), on the goroutine that received the packet from WireGuard. There is no queue between the filter and gVisor, so a packet that passed the filter is never dropped for lack of queue room; a slow stack slows the receive path. Merged: pump_ingress (ts_runtime/src/netstack_actor.rs) moves packets into a flume ring of 4096 packets and 4096*MTU bytes with try_send, and drops any packet that does not fit, after it was decrypted and passed the filter. The drop is logged at debug only, and both production callers (netstack_actor.rs and forwarder_actor.rs) discard the count pump_ingress returns, so nothing counts it. The PR's reason for dropping is real: the queue ahead of the pump, OverlayFromDataplane in ts_runtime/src/dataplane.rs, is an unbounded mpsc, so waiting would only move the backlog there. That unbounded queue is itself the structural difference from upstream. Closing the gap means bounding the dataplane queue so pressure reaches the receive path, or recording the ring as an intended difference and exporting the drop count as a metric.

findings.title: Netstack egress stays unbounded, where upstream caps each outbound queue at 512 packets and blocks the writer
findings.detail: Upstream: netstack.go builds the endpoint with newLinkEndpoint(512, ...), which gives each outbound queue a 512-slot channel. queue.Write blocks the gVisor writer until a slot frees or the queue closes, and WritePackets stops a batch early on ErrNoBufferSpace. So the stack-to-WireGuard queue is bounded and the stack is held back while it is full. Merged: WakingPipe::ingress_bounded keeps the device-to-caller direction on flume::unbounded, and the new test egress_is_not_bounded makes that a guarantee. The doc comment gives the reason that smoltcp's TxToken::consume is synchronous and cannot wait. smoltcp does have a way to push back without waiting: Device::transmit returns Option<TxToken>, and None makes the interface defer the packet to a later poll. WakingPipeDev::transmit (ts_netstack_smoltcp/src/pipe.rs) returns None only when the receiver is gone, never when the queue is deep. Replies a peer can provoke (RSTs, ACKs, ICMP) and local sends can therefore pile up without limit when the dataplane drains more slowly than smoltcp emits. That is the same memory growth the PR closed on ingress, and upstream bounds it. The port would bound the egress channel and have transmit() return None while it is full.
